# Exercises for Part II {.unnumbered #sec-exercises-london}



The first five exercises collect Part II's hands-on work in order. Each names the chapter
that explains it, how you know you are done, and the line that catches you up if you are not;
a checkpoint is the state at the *end* of its block, so after catching up, skip to the next
exercise. @sec-checkpoints has the whole table. If you did the chapters' steps, use these five
as a checklist: confirm each "done when" and move on. If you read without doing, do them here,
in order. The rest leave the prompts out. In the transfer
tasks you write the prompt and the check yourself, and the review questions test whether the
reasons stuck; short answers are at the end.

Start the assistant in `~/london-guide/`, next to `~/quarto-workshop/`. Catching up reads
outside that folder, so approve the assistant's request to read `../quarto-workshop`.

## Exercise II.1: London in Markdown {.unnumbered}

From @sec-markdown. Write `london.md` with a heading, lists, a link, the Big Ben photo with alt
text and credit, a quotation, a table from `data/sights.csv` and a code fence; render it and keep
a live preview; write the project's `AGENTS.md`; give the folder its own environment with uv.

::: done
`london.html` shows both lists, the photo with its credit, the five-row table and the checklist,
and `uv run quarto check jupyter` reports the Python in this folder's `.venv`.
:::

::: catchup
```default
Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/checkpoints/01-london-markdown/README.md
```
:::

## Exercise II.2: A document that computes {.unnumbered}

From @sec-compute. Rename the guide to `london.qmd` with front matter, add a cell that reads
`data/attractions.csv` and a sentence with inline code, add a captioned, labelled bar chart, then
render to HTML, Word and a Typst PDF (and, optionally, PowerPoint, EPUB and Reveal.js).

::: done
`london.html` shows the title block, the computed sentence and a numbered chart, and
`london.docx` and `london.pdf` show the same sentence and chart.
:::

::: catchup
```default
Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/checkpoints/02-london-qmd/README.md
```
:::

## Exercise II.3: Three audiences at once {.unnumbered}

From @sec-audiences. With one prompt and three sub-agents, write the dashboard, the Word brief
with its covering email, and the A5 flyer; the lead renders them one at a time.

::: done
`london-dashboard.html` has an Attractions page with three value boxes, a bar chart and a line
chart, and a Churches page listing ten churches with Visit London links; `london-email.docx`
opens with headings and working links; `london-email-message.md` holds the email in one text
block; `london-flyer.pdf` is one A5 page.
:::

::: catchup
```default
Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/checkpoints/04-london-audiences/README.md
```
:::

There is no checkpoint 03: the workshop's block numbering skips it.

## Exercise II.4: A published website {.unnumbered}

From @sec-publish. Make the folder a website with a navigation bar and a Downloads menu, put it
on GitHub, and publish it with an interactive `uv run quarto publish gh-pages`.

::: done
`https://<your-github-username>.github.io/london-guide/london-dashboard.html` opens on your phone.
:::

::: catchup
```default
Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/examples/london/README.md
```
:::

If you have already published, the catch-up copies the finished project's README over yours;
restore your own with `git checkout -- README.md`.

## Exercise II.5: Change an input, explain the rebuild {.unnumbered}

From @sec-london-change, with no prompt supplied. Set the Tower of London's `visits_2025` to
`8000000`, predict which outputs change, rebuild, explain what changed and what did not, and
restore the real value with `git restore data/attractions.csv`.

::: done
you can name the outputs that changed, the ones that did not, and the line of code that links
each changed output to the input. Model answers are in @sec-checkpoints.
:::

## Write your own prompts {.unnumbered #going-further}

These build on Part II and have no checkpoints. For each, write the prompt yourself, as
concrete as the book's (the files, the columns, the output) and ending with a check you can
verify without trusting the assistant's report. If you skipped them, the optional pieces come
first: the square advert (@sec-london-social), the white paper (@sec-london-whitepaper) and
the three.js page (@sec-london-3d).

1. **A handout of free attractions.** The office wants a one-page A5 handout of the
   attractions in `data/attractions.csv` that are free to enter, each with its 2025 visits.
   Decide which `admission` values count as free and say so in the prompt. You are done when
   the handout lists as many attractions as the dashboard's "Top 10 with free entry" value
   box counts, and no number on it was typed.
2. **Then and now.** Add a section to `london.qmd` comparing each of the five sights' 2025
   visits with 2019's, from `data/visits.csv`. Your prompt should say why 2019 is the year to
   compare with, and ask for the one sight whose counts are not like-for-like to be flagged.
   You are done when every percentage comes from a cell and the flagged sight is the one
   `data/README.md` names.
3. **Turn a copy into a computation.** The flyer and the sights tables in the guide and the
   partner brief all copy their facts from `data/sights.csv` (@tbl-london-deps). Make the flyer's table read the file instead. Your
   check: change one station name in `sights.csv` yourself, rebuild, and see it on the flyer.
   Restore the file afterwards.
4. **A map in two dimensions.** The 3-D map's data are in `data/places.csv` and the borough
   boundaries in `data/london-boroughs.geojson`. Add a third dashboard page that draws the
   sights and churches on a 2-D Plotly map from those files, with each point's source in its
   hover text. Decide how you will check that every point is where it should be.
5. **Update the live site.** Change the guide's welcome sentence, then write one prompt that
   commits with a message that says why and publishes the update with
   `uv run quarto publish gh-pages --no-prompt`. You are done when the new sentence is on
   your phone.

## Review questions {.unnumbered}

1. The project's rules say "ALVA member attractions", never "London's most visited
   attractions". What would be wrong with the second phrase?
2. A colleague copies your `london-guide/` folder without `.venv/`. What gives them the same
   packages as you, and what do they type first?
3. While `quarto preview` runs on `london.qmd`, the assistant runs `quarto render london.qmd`
   and it fails with `readfile 'london.quarto_ipynb'`. What happened, and what are two ways
   to avoid it?
4. In the guide's sentence about visits, which parts update when `attractions.csv` changes,
   and when? Does any part not update?
5. The guide's bar chart has a caption and alt text. What should each say, and why are they
   not the same?
6. You need two changes to `london-dashboard.qmd`: a new value box and a fix to the line
   chart's legend. Should you give them to two sub-agents working in parallel?
7. Why is the flyer's page size set with `papersize: a5`, but the square advert's in a raw
   Typst block?
8. Netlify can build your site from the repository, or you can render it yourself and upload
   it. Which does the London project need, and why?
9. After the rebuild in Exercise II.5, the dashboard on your computer shows the Tower of
   London as the most visited attraction, but the flyer has not changed and the dashboard on
   your phone still shows the old numbers. Explain both.

## Answers {.unnumbered}

1. ALVA counts only its member sites, so its table is not a list of every London
   attraction. "London's most visited attractions" would claim more than the data show
   (@sec-london-agents).
2. `uv.lock`, which records the exact version of every package for every system. Their first
   `uv run` command, such as `uv run quarto render london.md`, builds `.venv/` from it
   (@sec-environments).
3. A render writes a temporary notebook named after the file, and the preview was rendering
   the same file at the same moment, so the two collided. Let the preview do the rendering
   while it runs, or stop it with Ctrl+C first and restart it afterwards
   (@sec-render-mechanics).
4. The inline code (the top attraction, its visits and the total) updates at the next render,
   not when the file is saved. The word "ten" is typed, so it never updates (@sec-code-cells).
5. The caption says what the chart is: the measure, the year and whose attractions. The alt
   text says what it shows, such as which bar is longest and which shortest, for a reader who
   cannot see it (@sec-cell-options).
6. No. Both edit the same file, and both are small. Sub-agents suit independent, substantial
   tasks that write different files; make these two edits in turn (@sec-sub-agents).
7. Typst has a paper name for A5 but none for a 12 cm square, so the advert's size needs a raw
   block, which Quarto passes to Typst untouched. A raw block ties the source to one format,
   so use it only for what the format's settings cannot express (@sec-london-social).
8. Render it yourself and upload it: the pages run Python, and Quarto's Netlify build plugin
   runs none. A host that builds would also find no rendered site in the repository, because
   `.gitignore` leaves `_site/` out (@sec-hosting).
9. The flyer loads no data at all: its facts were copied into its Markdown, so a change to
   `attractions.csv` cannot reach it. The live site shows what was last published, and
   changes only when you publish again (@sec-london-change).

The second transfer task compares with 2019 because it is the last year before the pandemic
years 2020 and 2021, which `data/README.md` says are not comparable with the others. The sight
to flag is the Natural History Museum: from 2024 its count includes its reopened gardens.
